text: FEEDSTOCK AVAILABILITY AND SUPPLY CHAIN LOGISTICS The biomass resource data from the DOE 2023 Billion Ton study (DOE, 2024) was used to provide insights into the supply curves (availability and cost) of feedstocks to produce the alternative fuels studied here. The use of this dataset allows regional supply and demand analyses at a county level granularity across the United States. The BILT model was then used to optimize biorefinery facility siting to use these biomass resources with given constraints on spacing between plants and other economic or location constraints. The combination of the biomass resource data and the 64 BILT modeling allowed the project to quantify spatially explicit allocation of biomass resources to biorefineries for rail applicable biofuels given the TEAs and LCAs from the project. Insights from this work include information about the size of biorefineries needed for the different pathways and locations of biorefineries that could be supported by regional feedstock distributions. Identifying renewable and scalable feedstock sources through studies like this are key to supporting large-scale fuel production. This analysis did not account for existing refueling depots or facilities other than the existing petroleum facilities and soybean processing facilities and only optimized for new sites. Additional research could better link existing facilities. Additional research is also needed to link the demand side to biomass pricing, and to understand the tradeoffs for the pathways that compete for the biomass resources and facilities. For example, many of the pathways investigated here rely on the same feedstock and others could be implemented simultaneously (e.g. corn to ethanol + stover to ethanol + woody to RD + soybean to RD). Additional research would be valuable in understanding which combination of pathways most benefits a set of objectives. Biofuels require multiple preprocessing steps such as drying, densifying, chemical pretreatment, and esterifying. The impacts of preprocessing hub for feedstocks before sending them to refineries should be analyzed. Depending on the presence or absence of the preprocessing units, the cost of biofuel production could be significantly different. 7.7 TECHNOLOGICAL INTEGRATION AND SYSTEMS ANALYSIS Future research should explore the integration of alternative fuels into existing rail systems, considering both technical and operational aspects of integration. This includes analyzing systems to evaluate the impacts of fuel transitions on rail infrastructure, operations, and maintenance. Understanding these interactions will help identify potential barriers and opportunities for seamless integration. 7.8 REGIONAL FUEL DEMAND ANALYSIS This study analyzed the U.S. freight rail system to understand regional freight rail energy use and identify potential alternative fuel corridors. Due to data limitations in FAF and CWS, a combined dataset was created using an iterative proportional fitting statistical technique to estimate county level-freight movements. These movements were routed on the North American Rail Network using the shortest path algorithm to calculate link-level tonnages, state-level ton-miles, and future flows. These analyses identified corridors with high tonnage concentration, and those projected to have increasing tonnages.
